course: Strongest:

Covers everything needed to grasp single variable calculus.

Weakest:

The exams are artificially and unnecessarily hard, this discourages students from appreciating an otherwise important discipline. Some questions are downright sadistic. (Compare them to an MIT midterm for instance) Only 1 hour and 40 minutes are allowed in an exam.
The pace of the course is somewhat unreasonable.

The textbook by the late Stewart chosen for this course is universally acknowledged as being one of the worst calculus textbooks ever conceived with the most laughable number of editions with infinitesimal changes.

It's heavily computational and it is solely directed to engineers. The course's aim is not to teach fundamentals of mathematics despite its name "MATH" 101. When asked why we weren't taught the precise definition of limits, the teacher said "because engineers don't really care".

course: The curriculum for this course doesn't make much sense, particularly for non-engineering and Math majors. It's excessive and covers far too many topics. The class sizes are large, and there's a lack of one-on-one interactions. The course isn't designed for students; it's completely divorced from the needs of students, of the things that they're interested in and would benefit from, both personally and in their individual fields. The idea of a 'zero-tolerance' policy that makes no exceptions for things like internet connectivity and other technological issues  makes absolutely no sense, particularly during a pandemic. There's a built in assumption that students are attempting to cheat their way through the course, which is to the detriment of all those involved in teaching and learning. It's not a constructive learning environment, it's taxing and disheartening and unfair.
